stem: A 21-year-old healthy woman asks about her own risk after her 3-year-old sister is diagnosed with cystic fibrosis by a positive sweat chloride test. Both parents are healthy, she has no symptoms, and she has not had genetic testing.
oneliner: 21F + healthy + 3-year-old sister with cystic fibrosis + healthy parents + untested → what carrier probability?
ask: What is the probability that she is a carrier of a cystic fibrosis mutation?

whyNot.A: That is the **population** carrier frequency; with an **affected sibling** her risk is much higher
whyNot.B: That is the chance of being **affected** at conception; she is **known to be unaffected**
whyNot.C: That is her risk before her **healthy status** is used; excluding the affected outcome raises it
whyNot.E: That is the chance of being **unaffected**, not the chance of being a carrier

why: An affected child of two healthy parents means both parents are **carriers** of an **autosomal recessive** gene. Their children are 1/4 affected, 1/2 carrier and 1/4 unaffected non-carrier. She is **known to be unaffected**, so only the last two groups remain: 2 carrier parts out of 3, a risk of **2/3**.

idea.rule: Healthy sibling of a patient with an autosomal recessive disease: carrier risk is 2/3 (2 of the 3 unaffected outcomes).
also: Two carrier parents give 1/4 affected, 1/2 carrier, 1/4 unaffected non-carrier
Her chance of an affected child with an untested unrelated partner is 2/3 × 1/25 × 1/4 = 1/150
The same 2/3 rule applies to sickle cell disease, PKU and Tay-Sachs
Remove the affected outcome before counting carriers in a healthy sibling

stem: A 2-year-old white girl has had repeated pneumonia since infancy and passes greasy, foul-smelling stools. A sweat chloride test confirms the diagnosis and she is started on fat-soluble vitamin supplements. In her population the disease affects 1 in 2500 people.
oneliner: 2F + recurrent pneumonia + greasy stools + positive sweat chloride + incidence 1 in 2500 whites → what carrier frequency?
ask: What is the approximate carrier frequency in this population?

whyNot.A: That is the carrier chance for a child of one carrier parent, not a **population** frequency
whyNot.C: That is **q**, the mutant allele frequency; carriers are **2pq**, about twice that
whyNot.D: That is the **square of the carrier frequency**, not the carrier frequency itself
whyNot.E: That is the **disease incidence (q²)**, given in the stem, not the carrier frequency

why: An incidence of **1/2500 = q²**, so **q = 1/50** and p is about 1. The carrier frequency is **2pq ≈ 2q = 1/25**.

idea.rule: Autosomal recessive disease: q² = incidence, and carriers ≈ 2q.
also: Allele frequency q is the square root of the incidence
About 1 in 25 white people carries a cystic fibrosis mutation
Hardy-Weinberg needs random mating and no selection or migration
X-linked recessive disease: male incidence equals q

stem: A 38-year-old man who has never smoked has had two years of worsening breathlessness. CT shows emphysema that is worst at the lung bases, and his liver enzymes are mildly raised. Liver biopsy shows diastase-resistant PAS-positive globules in hepatocytes, and his serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level is very low.
oneliner: 38M + never-smoker + basal emphysema + raised liver enzymes + PAS-positive globules in hepatocytes + very low alpha-1 antitrypsin → which genotype?
ask: Which SERPINA1 genotype most likely explains this?

whyNot.A: PiMM is the **normal** genotype with a normal enzyme level, not a **very low** one
whyNot.B: PiMS gives only a mild fall (about 80% of normal) and usually causes **no disease**
whyNot.C: PiMZ leaves about 60% of normal enzyme; disease is mild or absent, not a **very low level** with hepatic globules
whyNot.D: PiSS leaves roughly 60% of the enzyme and causes little disease; this man's level is **very low**

why: Basal **panacinar emphysema** in a **never-smoker** with **PAS-positive hepatocyte globules** is alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The **Z** protein misfolds and is retained in the hepatocyte, so a **ZZ** homozygote has the **lowest serum level** and develops both lung disease (unopposed neutrophil elastase) and liver disease.

idea.rule: PiZZ = lowest alpha-1 antitrypsin = emphysema in the lung and liver disease from retained protein.
also: SERPINA1 lies on chromosome 14 and is inherited codominantly
Misfolded Z protein piles up in the hepatocyte ER, forming PAS-positive diastase-resistant globules
Without the antiprotease, neutrophil elastase destroys alveolar elastin
Smoking brings on emphysema earlier in affected patients

stem: A 45-year-old East Asian woman who has never smoked has a 3-cm mass at the periphery of the lung. Biopsy shows a gland-forming adenocarcinoma with mucin, and the mass shrinks markedly on an oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor.
oneliner: 45F + East Asian + never-smoker + peripheral gland-forming adenocarcinoma + shrinks on oral tyrosine kinase inhibitor → which driver gene?
ask: Which gene is most likely altered in this tumor?

whyNot.A: RB1 loss is typical of **small cell carcinoma**, a central neuroendocrine tumor, not a **gland-forming** one
whyNot.B: L-myc amplification occurs in **small cell carcinoma** and offers no kinase target for an **oral inhibitor**
whyNot.D: TP53 is a tumor suppressor with **no kinase to block**, so it does not explain the **response to a kinase inhibitor**
whyNot.E: BMPR2 mutations cause **heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension**, not a lung adenocarcinoma

why: A **never-smoking** woman of East Asian descent with a **peripheral adenocarcinoma** classically has an **activating EGFR mutation** (or an ALK rearrangement). The tumor depends on that signal, so it shrinks on an **EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor**. KRAS mutations are commoner in smokers.

idea.rule: Lung adenocarcinoma in never-smokers: EGFR mutation or ALK rearrangement, treatable with oral kinase inhibitors.
also: ALK rearrangements respond to ALK inhibitors such as crizotinib
KRAS-mutant tumors are commoner in smokers and do not respond to EGFR inhibitors
EGFR-mutant disease is commoner in women and East Asian patients
Adenocarcinoma is the lung cancer most often seen in never-smokers
